03-how-the-industry-works.title: Where the money goes in a typical brokerage transaction
03-how-the-industry-works.standfirst: Many first-time buyers reach this market through a family office, yet only a quarter of Swiss single family offices manage a boat or aircraft in-house. Such a buyer may come to a sale without specialist advice, on a EUR 28 m deal that carries EUR 1.7 to 2.8 million in commission, and is rarely told which commission scale applies.

blocks.text: Who the buyer is, and who advises them

Many first-time buyers reach this market through a family office. The typical Swiss single family office is a lean investment shop, median five people, and running a yacht is outside its expertise. Only a quarter of Swiss single family offices manage a boat or aircraft in-house, and nearly half do not offer the service at all.

blocks.caption: What a Swiss single family office does in-house, and what it does not. Swiss single family offices, survey of 82 offices, about 27 percent of the roughly 300 in Switzerland.
head: Function
How the office handles it
What it means for a first purchase
rows: Median 5 staff in Switzerland; 61 percent run 1–5
A small expert team, not a department with a yacht specialist
Offered in-house by more than 60 percent
The office runs the family’s money itself
For specialist matters the office already reaches outside
In-house 25 percent, outsourced 27 percent, not offered 48 percent
The yacht is the one asset the office is least set up to run
blocks.sourceLine: University of St. Gallen, Swiss Institute of Banking and Finance, with SFOA and UBS, The Swiss Single Family Office Landscape 2026.

blocks.text: An independent adviser can fill this gap. An office set up to preserve the family’s capital is not equipped to run a refit, vet a broker, or check a sale-and-purchase agreement against the commission scales set out below. Where it does not have that expertise in-house, it can engage an outside specialist, as it already does for succession and legal work.
Two commission scales

blocks.caption: On a EUR 28 m sale of a 40 m yacht. Both scales are presented as “the standard” by the brokers using them. They are not the same.

blocks.text: Refit yards, by region

The over-30 m refit market is concentrated in four regions: the Western Mediterranean (Spain, France, Italy), Northern Europe (UK, Netherlands, Germany), the Eastern Mediterranean (Turkey) and the US Eastern Seaboard. Top European yards are typically booked 12 to 24 months ahead for major refits; US East Coast lead times are shorter but tightening, particularly at Rybovich and Derecktor.

07-operations.title: Crew pay, insurance and charter regimes
07-operations.standfirst: Crew is 30 to 40 percent of annual operating cost on a typical 50m, by far the largest single line. Hull rates rose from 2022, peaked in 2024 and have since softened; after Bayesian, underwriters looked harder at crew procedures and stability rather than raising rates across the board. The commercial charter regimes are set out country by country.

blocks.text: Captain pay, by yacht size

blocks.caption: Captain pay rises with size. Quay Crew records 7 percent growth in the 70 to 79 m bracket since its 2023 survey; 63 percent of captains surveyed are on time-for-time rotation.
head: Yacht size

blocks.sourceLine: YPI Crew 2026 salary guide; Quay Crew 2025 captain survey; Erica Lay (EL Crew Co) on senior-captain salary premiums.

blocks.caption: War risk in practice.

rows.label: What it covers
rows.value: Unexpected damage from riots, uprisings, vandalism or political incident while the yacht is outside high-risk zones. It does not cover the yacht inside designated War Risk areas.
rows.note: Reference incidents: MY Kaos, vandalised alongside the dock in Barcelona (2023), and damage during the 2016 Turkish coup attempt.

rows.label: Entering an exclusion zone
rows.value: An additional premium (AP), set by motor or sail, maximum cruising speed, freeboard height, appearance, length of stay in the area, and the captain and crew’s experience of the route. Increased deductibles often apply inside the zone.
rows.note: Fifty percent of the AP is typically returned as a no-claims discount after a successful transit.

rows.label: High-risk passages
rows.value: Insurers normally require a separate Kidnap & Ransom policy and armed security from a partnered or accredited provider, both at the owner’s cost.

rows.label: Notice of cancellation
rows.value: Since the Ukraine and Middle East conflicts, insurers have issued seven-day notice of cancellation on H&M and P&I in respect of certain cruising areas. Cover can usually be bought back for an additional premium if the owner intends to visit.
rows.note: Ask before the itinerary is fixed.

blocks.sourceLine: Ollie Davis, PIB Marine, interviewed for this chapter (May 2026).

blocks.text: Commercial charter regimes, by jurisdiction

blocks.caption: Commercial registration is decided jurisdiction by jurisdiction; there is no single global licence. The VAT regimes that interact with charter are in chapter 4.

rows.label: France
rows.value: French Commercial Exemption (FCE): commercial registration, full-time crew, length above 15 m.
rows.note: Its VAT conditions, including the share of voyages leaving French waters and the limit on static charter use, are set out in chapter 4.

rows.label: Italy
rows.value: Italian flag with commercial registration, or a non-Italian flag meeting Codice della Nautica conditions. VAT on charter fees is 22 percent on the portions in Italian waters.
rows.note: Italian leasing and its effective-use test: chapter 4.

rows.label: Spain
rows.value: Royal Decrees 186/2023 and 587/2024 replace the charter licence with an Affidavit of Responsibility filed with the Harbour Master, for EU and non-EU flags alike; 2026 is the transition year.
rows.note: Spanish residents and entities established in Spain register yachts locally and pay the special tax on certain means of transport at 12 percent of value (11 percent in the Canary Islands); yachts used exclusively for charter can be exempt, subject to conditions on use by owners and their families.

rows.label: Greece
rows.value: Historically the most restrictive in the Mediterranean. Greek-flagged and EU-flagged yachts above 35 m can charter under the standard regime. Since February 2024 the e-Charter Permission also lets non-EU-flagged commercial yachts over 35 m with non-wooden hulls charter in Greek waters for up to 28 days a year, subject to a special fee and VAT registration.
rows.note: NEPA is the long-form route.

rows.label: Croatia
rows.value: Croatian flag or a local charter-agency arrangement under the Croatian Maritime Code. Annual permit.
rows.note: 13 percent VAT on charter fees.

rows.label: Turkey
rows.value: “Blue Cruise” charter requires Turkish-flag operation or a Turkish charter agreement with a licensed local operator.
rows.note: Foreign-flagged yachts can cruise privately; commercial charter requires the local licence.

rows.label: Monaco
rows.value: The Monégasque flag permits up to 90 days of commercial charter a year without personal tax levies on the owner; under several neighbouring EU flags the same vessel would face VAT on private owner use.
rows.note: Visible reflagging at brokerage during 2026 on yachts of 30 to 50 m with light charter intent (Capt. Ukic of M/Y Ellen, MYBA Charter Show 2026, in The Superyacht Report).

rows.label: Cayman Islands and Marshall Islands
rows.value: Both issue commercial certificates covering global charter activity. Cayman applies the Red Ensign Group Yacht Code (July 2024 edition), the Marshall Islands its own Yacht Code (2026 edition).
rows.note: The dominant choices for over-30 m commercial programmes.

rows.label: Malta
rows.value: An EU charter route widely used for long Mediterranean seasons.
rows.note: VAT on a lease under the Maltese leasing guidelines (in force since March 2020) follows documented use: chapter 4.

rows.label: United States
rows.value: Regulated under federal law (Coast Guard and the Passenger Vessel Services Act, part of the US cabotage rules often grouped with the Jones Act). Foreign-flagged yachts cannot carry passengers between US ports under standard charter, which severely restricts non-US-flagged commercial operation in US waters.
rows.note: The US tax treatment of a charter business is in the chapter essay.

blocks.sourceLine: Royal Decrees 186/2023 and 587/2024 (Spain); Greek e-Charter Permission (February 2024); Red Ensign Group Yacht Code (July 2024); Marshall Islands Yacht Code (2026); The Superyacht Report (Monaco).
